name: Te Pae Christchurch Convention Centre
access_notes: PCEE 2027 venue, 16-18 February 2027. Public foyers open during events.
summary: The PCEE 2027 venue. A steel-framed convention centre split into three structurally independent buildings, wrapped in a 42,000-tile facade that traces Canterbury's braided rivers.
story:
Te Pae replaced the convention centre demolished after the 2011 earthquake and opened in December 2021 as an anchor project of the central-city rebuild. It holds a 1,400-seat tiered auditorium that divides in two, up to 3,300 m² of exhibition space and 24 meeting rooms.

Holmes divided the 15,000 m² footprint into three structurally independent but interconnected buildings. Bracing lines sit roughly 30-40 m apart so the auditorium, exhibition hall and banquet spaces stay brace-free, with floor and roof plates transferring seismic load between them. The designers note that seismic loads here are more than 50 times the wind loads the international team was used to working with.

The facade is 42,058 herringbone fibre-cement tiles on 1,604 panels. To keep the ribbons flowing across several floors, the team avoided the usual horizontal slip joint at each level and hid vertical movement joints within the tiling instead. Inside, the auditorium roof was erected without props around a central spine truss.
architect: Woods Bagot with Warren and Mahoney

name: Tūranga (Christchurch Central Library)
access_notes: Open library hours, free entry. Take the lift or stairs to the Level 4 roof gardens (Ngā Māra); the south garden overlooks Cathedral Square and the Cathedral reinstatement works.
summary: Christchurch's central library, opened in 2018. Post-tensioned concrete walls rock on their foundations and re-centre, with dampers absorbing the energy. Head up to the Level 4 roof gardens: the south one looks straight across Cathedral Square to the Cathedral.
story:
Tūranga opened on 12 October 2018, replacing the central library that closed on the day of the February 2011 earthquake. At about 9,850 m² over five storeys it is the largest public library in the South Island.

Its seismic system is a set of large post-tensioned concrete walls. High-strength tendons clamp each wall to its foundation with roughly 1,000 tonnes of force. In a large earthquake the walls rock on their base, and the tendons pull them back to plumb, so the building self-centres rather than being left with residual drift.

Twenty lead-extrusion dampers, each about a metre long and 185 kg, sit between the walls and the foundations. They were developed by University of Canterbury researcher Geoffrey Rodgers, and viscous dampers add further energy dissipation. A steel moment frame wraps the perimeter. The design won an Institution of Structural Engineers Structural Award in 2019.

Don't leave without going up to Level 4, where two roof gardens, Ngā Māra, open off the creativity floor. The north garden looks out over Gloucester Street. The south garden faces Cathedral Square and gives one of the best views in the city of the Cathedral and its reinstatement works, a good place to see the next stop before you walk to it.

name: Christchurch Art Gallery Te Puna o Waiwhetū
address: Cnr Worcester Blvd and Montreal St
access_notes: Open gallery hours, free entry. Look for the tiled moat around the perimeter.
summary: Liquefaction left the gallery up to 182 mm out of level. Engineers strengthened the ground, re-levelled the building and slid isolators in beneath it. Finished in 2015, it was the South Island's first base-isolation retrofit.
story:
Designed by David Cole of the Buchan Group after a competition that drew more than 90 entries, the gallery opened in 2003. After the February 2011 earthquake it served as the city's Civil Defence headquarters.

Deep liquefaction had caused differential settlement. The raft foundation protected the superstructure, but it sank unevenly across the 6,500 m² plan by up to 182 mm. Mainmark-Uretek first strengthened the ground with jet grouting, then re-levelled the building with a computer-controlled 'jack on grout' injection system.

Aurecon then designed a base-isolation retrofit. More than 130 isolators were installed in the basement, several structural elements were strengthened, and a 600 mm moat was formed around the building at ground level so it can move. Completed in December 2015, it was the first base-isolation retrofit in the South Island. Walk the perimeter to find the moat's cover tiles.

name: Christchurch Cathedral
access_notes: Fenced construction site - exterior viewing from Cathedral Square only.
summary: Christchurch's Gothic Revival stone cathedral, wrecked in 2011. It is now being repaired, strengthened and base isolated, an approach the engineers say has seldom been attempted on a damaged stone building anywhere.
story:
Designed by George Gilbert Scott and built under Benjamin Mountfort's supervision, the nave was consecrated in 1881 and the cathedral was completed in 1904. The February 2011 earthquake brought down the spire and the upper tower, and later aftershocks destroyed the west wall's rose window.

After years of debate, the decision to reinstate rather than demolish was made in 2017. Holmes is the structural engineer and Warren and Mahoney the architect. The scheme stabilises and repairs the masonry, adds a new seismic frame and floor system, and places the whole building on base isolation. That is expected to cut earthquake accelerations reaching the structure to about a third.

Work paused in 2024 for lack of funding. In September 2025 a staged plan was announced: reinstate the tower, nave and west wall (including the Rose Window) first, the same areas that opened in 1881, giving seating for about 700. This halves the funding gap, and the cathedral could reopen by the end of 2030.
architect: George Gilbert Scott; reinstatement by Warren and Mahoney

name: Christchurch Town Hall
access_notes: Foyers open during performances and events.
summary: Warren and Mahoney's 1972 modernist landmark beside the Avon. Lateral spreading damaged it badly. It was saved by injecting more than 1,000 jet-grout columns beneath it and casting a new raft foundation, then reopened in 2019.
story:
Designed by Miles Warren and Maurice Mahoney, the Town Hall opened in 1972. Its Douglas Lilburn Auditorium is internationally known for its acoustics. The 2010-2011 earthquakes caused liquefaction and lateral spreading towards the river, damaging the foundations and pulling the building out of level.

Holmes and Tonkin + Taylor worked together on the remediation, part of a conservation project of more than $167 million. First, 1,098 jet-grout columns were injected through the existing floor to stabilise the ground. The floor was then removed and replaced with a new raft foundation 700-900 mm thick, tying the existing foundations together. The superstructure was then re-levelled and strengthened to 100% of the New Building Standard.

The Town Hall reopened on 23 February 2019, eight years and a day after the earthquake. The project won an Institution of Structural Engineers Structural Award in 2021.

name: The Arts Centre Te Matatiki Toi Ora
access_notes: Courtyards and many buildings open daily. Some areas may be closed for restoration.
summary: The former Canterbury College campus: 23 Gothic Revival stone buildings, 21 of them Category 1 heritage. Their post-quake restoration, valued at around $290 million, is one of the largest heritage restoration programmes in the world.
story:
Begun in 1877 to designs by Benjamin Mountfort and later architects, the site was Canterbury College (now the University of Canterbury) until the 1970s, when it became an arts precinct. The 2010-2011 earthquakes damaged the buildings extensively.

The restoration programme has strengthened the masonry buildings while keeping the work out of sight. At the Great Hall (1882), with Holmes as engineer, old external post-tensioning was removed. New high-strength bars were installed both horizontally and vertically within the walls, then grouted, so the strengthening sits hidden behind the original fabric. The Great Hall reopened in June 2016.

The programme has won national and international structural and heritage awards, including an Institution of Structural Engineers Structural Award in 2017 for Block C (the Great Hall and Clock Tower). Work continues, including the rebuild of the Observatory Tower.

name: Transitional (Cardboard) Cathedral
access_notes: Open most days for visitors outside service times - check before visiting.
summary: Shigeru Ban's 'Cardboard Cathedral': 96 cardboard tubes, each 600 mm across, form an A-frame. Because the tubes alone couldn't carry the load, a timber LVL beam was threaded through or alongside each one. The building opened in 2013.
story:
With the stone cathedral out of use, the Anglican diocese commissioned Japanese architect Shigeru Ban, working pro bono with Warren and Mahoney, to build a transitional cathedral. It opened in August 2013, seats about 700, and rises 21 m above the altar.

The A-frame is formed from 96 cardboard tubes, each 600 mm in diameter, coated with waterproof polyurethane and fire retardant and spaced so daylight filters through. Local manufacturers could not produce tubes long or strong enough to work structurally on their own. Holmes therefore threaded a laminated veneer lumber (LVL) beam through, or alongside, each tube, so the timber carries the load and the cardboard forms the architecture.

Eight shipping containers form the side walls at the base, and a polycarbonate roof keeps the weather out. Reports put the building at around 130% of the New Building Standard. The triangular stained-glass west window draws on images from the stone cathedral's Rose Window.
architect: Shigeru Ban with Warren and Mahoney

name: Christchurch Justice and Emergency Services Precinct
access_notes: Public foyer during business hours. Security screening applies.
summary: Courts, police, fire, ambulance and emergency management under one roof. Four steel buildings sit on a shared base-isolated podium, designed to Importance Level 4 so emergency services can keep working after a major quake.
story:
The precinct opened on 12 September 2017 as the first major Crown anchor project of the rebuild. It cost about $300 million and has around 40,000 m² of floor area. It brings together the District Court, Police, Corrections, Fire and Emergency, St John and the National Emergency Management Agency, the largest multi-agency government co-location in New Zealand.

Its four buildings are seismically separated, two-way steel moment-resisting frames. All four stand on a common podium that is base isolated at first-floor level using isolators and PTFE sliders, so in an earthquake they move together as one.

As an Importance Level 4 facility, it was designed with performance-based checks at 500-year, 2,500-year and 7,500-year return periods. The aim is that the agencies who respond to a disaster can keep working through and after it.
architect: Warren and Mahoney, Cox Architecture and Opus

name: Forte Health
access_notes: Private hospital - foyer only. Please respect patients and staff.
summary: Two generations of low-damage design on one site. The 2014 hospital was New Zealand's first steel PRESSS building, with rocking braced frames that re-centre. Its new four-storey expansion uses 48 self-centring friction braces that need no repair after an earthquake.
story:
Construction of this three-storey private hospital began in September 2012, and it opened in February 2014. It contains four operating theatres along with radiology and specialist clinics, and was one of the first major new buildings in the post-quake central city.

Alan Reay Consultants adapted the PRESSS (PREcast Seismic Structural Systems) rocking concept, previously used with precast concrete and engineered timber, to structural steel. The lateral system is coupled steel braced frames, post-tensioned vertically with unbonded high-strength bars. In a large earthquake the frames rock, and the post-tensioning pulls them back to centre.

Energy is dissipated by two types of replaceable fuse: University of Canterbury-developed lead-extrusion devices, used here in a building for the first time, and mild-steel yielding dampers. The engineers say combining the two had not been done before. The design targets immediate occupancy after an event like the 2010-2011 earthquakes.

The hospital is now growing again. A four-storey expansion of about 6,200 m², with piling completed in October 2025, is designed to Importance Level 4, the level required of buildings that must keep operating after a disaster. Lewis Bradford is the structural engineer.

Its lateral system uses 48 Tectonus DMAX seismic braces, with capacities from 1,500 to 2,650 kN. Inside each brace, grooved steel plates are clamped together by disc springs. In an earthquake the plates slide over one another, dissipating energy through friction, and the groove shape and springs push them back to their starting position afterwards, leaving almost no residual drift. Because there is no yielding steel fuse to replace, the braces are designed to come through an earthquake and its aftershocks without repair.

Compared with conventional eccentrically braced frames, the DMAX solution cut the peak pile tension demand by about 17% (1,200 kN to 1,000 kN) and peak pile compression by about 17.5% (2,000 kN to 1,650 kN).

name: Riverside Market
access_notes: Open daily, market hours. Good stop for lunch.
summary: A seven-day indoor food market built where the Re:START shipping-container mall stood after the earthquakes. It is fitted out largely in natural materials, including timber recycled from Lyttelton's wharves.
story:
After the 2011 earthquake, this block next to City Mall was cleared and hosted Re:START, the shipping-container shopping mall that kept retail alive in the red-zoned central city. Riverside Market opened on the same site on 28 September 2019.

The $80 million development was designed by Kirk Roberts Consulting for Mainland Capital and modelled on the food halls of Melbourne and Copenhagen. Market stalls fill the ground floor, and bars and restaurants on the first floor look down over them. The interior uses mostly natural materials, including timber recycled from the wharf at Lyttelton.

It averages more than 10,000 visitors a day and won the Property Council's retail award in 2020. It is a convenient refuelling stop mid-walk.

name: Isaac Theatre Royal
access_notes: Interior by ticket or guided tour only. The facade is best seen from Gloucester St.
summary: An Edwardian theatre rebuilt behind its own facade. The 1908 front was strengthened in place while monitored for movement. Behind it, new steel-and-concrete walls and a lightweight steel roof replaced the brick auditorium, and the dome and plasterwork were put back.
story:
The theatre opened in 1908 and was badly damaged in 2011. Its restoration, completed in November 2014, kept the heritage fabric but replaced almost everything structural behind it.

The 1908 facade and main stair were strengthened and rebuilt in place, with Harrison Grierson monitoring them for movement throughout. Behind them, the auditorium's brick walls were replaced with new steel and concrete walls. A lightweight steel roof went in above the reinstated plaster ceiling, and the dome was carefully removed and reinstated. The auditorium, foyers and egress routes now meet current building codes.

The team included Holmes (structural and fire engineering), Warren and Mahoney (architect), RCP (project manager) and Naylor Love (builder). The project received a national heritage award.

name: Christchurch Hospital Waipapa
access_notes: Active hospital - public foyer only. Please keep clear of clinical areas.
summary: A 62,000 m² acute hospital on 129 base isolators, with up to 650 mm of movement allowed between the lower-ground and ground floors. It was designed to Importance Level 4 so it can keep treating patients immediately after a major earthquake.
story:
Waipapa was completed in 2020 at a project value of around $500 million. It houses the emergency department, intensive care, 12 operating theatres and procedure rooms, and more than 400 inpatient beds, with a helipad on the roof.

The whole building sits on 129 base isolators, which allow as much as 650 mm of movement between the lower-ground and ground floors. Above the isolation plane, Holmes designed a steel moment frame from prefabricated sections bolted together on site. This minimised site welding and disruption on a live hospital campus.

As an Importance Level 4 facility it has to stay fully operational after a major earthquake. The low-damage approach therefore extended beyond the structure to building services, fit-out and contents, which were also seismically detailed.
architect: Chow:Hill, Warren and Mahoney and Thinc Health

name: Te Kaha One New Zealand Stadium
access_notes: Interior on event days only. The exterior and roof are visible from Madras and Hereford Streets.
summary: Christchurch's new covered stadium, opened in March 2026. A 175 x 211 m ETFE roof spans the pitch. Eccentrically braced frames with replaceable fuses and buckling-restrained braces resist earthquakes, including 12 m roof BRBs that are the largest made in NZ.
story:
Te Kaha, meaning 'the strength' and gifted by Ngāi Tūāhuriri, opened on 27 March 2026. It replaces Lancaster Park, lost to the 2011 earthquake, and is described as the final piece of the central-city rebuild. It seats 25,000, expandable to 30,000, and up to 37,000 for concerts. It set its record crowd of 29,152 for the All Blacks against France in July 2026.

The fixed roof spans 175 m by 211 m on 40 perimeter columns arranged radially. Twelve lenticular trusses span across the pitch, and double-layer ETFE cushions let in enough daylight to grow natural turf.

A site-specific seismic hazard assessment found that design actions could be 15-45% higher than the code values. Mott MacDonald responded with eccentrically braced frames with replaceable fuses and with buckling-restrained braces. The roof BRBs are 12 m long, the largest ever made and tested in New Zealand.

name: Canterbury Museum
access_notes: Closed for redevelopment - view the works from Rolleston Ave. The museum's pop-up is at 66 Gloucester St.
summary: Mountfort's Gothic Revival museum and the 1932 Robert McDougall Gallery are being strengthened and placed on base isolation, with a new base-isolated basement and building between them. It is one of the most complex heritage retrofits under way in the country.
story:
Canterbury Museum opened on Rolleston Avenue in 1870, in stone buildings by Benjamin Mountfort that face the Cathedral down the length of Worcester Boulevard. It closed in 2022 for a redevelopment now costed at about $247 million, designed by Athfield Architects and built by Leighs Construction.

The plan base-isolates the heritage buildings, the Robert McDougall Gallery and the new building. A new base-isolated basement will protect a collection of more than 2.3 million items. Building it in a high water table, beneath and between heritage structures, is the hardest part of the job.

At the 1932 Robert McDougall Gallery, Holmes engineers had more than 300 micropiles drilled 11 m into the ground, over 3 km of them in total. The whole gallery was temporarily carried on them while the old basement was removed and rebuilt, before its weight was transferred onto new base isolation. The museum is due to reopen in 2028-29.
architect: Benjamin Mountfort; redevelopment by Athfield Architects

name: Quake City
access_notes: Open 10am-5pm daily. Entry charge applies; under-15s free with an adult.
summary: Canterbury Museum's exhibition on the 2010-2011 earthquakes, a short walk from Te Pae. It covers the science of the quakes, a hands-on liquefaction model, and objects that have come to define the disaster, including the top of the Cathedral spire.
story:
Quake City first opened in February 2013 in the Re:START shipping-container mall on Cashel Street. More than 190,000 people visited there before it moved to its current site, on the corner of Durham St North and Armagh St, in September 2017.

The exhibition traces the September 2010 and February 2011 earthquakes and their aftermath. It covers the response of emergency services, international rescue teams and volunteers, and the resilience of Canterbury's communities. A hands-on interactive shows how liquefaction happens, and the objects on display include the top of the ChristChurch Cathedral spire.

It is a good first stop to set the scene before the engineering sites. It is also next to the Canterbury Provincial Council Buildings, whose Stone Chamber collapsed in 2011.

name: CTV Building site memorial
access_notes: Open public memorial garden. Please be respectful - this is a place of remembrance.
summary: The CTV Building collapsed on 22 February 2011, killing 115 people - the majority of the earthquake's 185 deaths. The site is now a memorial garden. The Royal Commission found that the building's design was deficient and should not have been approved.
story:
The CTV Building was a reinforced concrete office building completed in 1987. It collapsed in the February 2011 earthquake, and 115 people died, including staff of the CTV television station and many students and teachers at King's Education language school. It was the greatest single loss of life in the disaster.

The Canterbury Earthquakes Royal Commission held an eight-week hearing into the collapse, with evidence from more than 80 witnesses. It found that the structural design was deficient and that the building should not have been granted a permit. The collapse and the Commission's findings remain a central case for New Zealand engineers on design competence, supervision and independent review.

The Crown bought the site, and it reopened as a memorial garden on the eve of the seventh anniversary in 2018. It is planted with cherry trees and native plants, with a stone plinth and running water, and keeps traces of the original building.

name: Canterbury Earthquake National Memorial
address: Ōtākaro Avon River, downstream of Montreal St bridge
access_notes: Open public space on both banks of the river.
summary: The national memorial to the 185 people who died in the 22 February 2011 earthquake. It sits on both banks of the Ōtākaro Avon River and opened on the sixth anniversary in 2017.
story:
Oi Manawa opened on 22 February 2017. It spans both banks of the Ōtākaro Avon River just downstream of the Montreal Street bridge, with a memorial wall bearing the names of the 185 people who died, and a sheltered amphitheatre-shaped space for reflection on the north bank.

The memorial cost about $11 million, funded mostly by the government with a contribution from the Christchurch Earthquake Mayoral Relief Fund. Each year on the anniversary, all 185 names are read aloud and the bell of HMNZS Canterbury is tolled for each one.

It is a natural place to pause on a walk about earthquake engineering, as a reminder of who the codes and the low-damage systems on this tour are ultimately for.

name: Akin Cafe
access_notes: Mon-Fri 7am-3pm, Sat-Sun 8am-3pm
summary: A daytime cafe at the top of High Street, set up by designers and architects. Good for a coffee and something from the cabinet between sites.

name: Belle
access_notes: Mon-Fri 7am-4pm, Sat-Sun 8am-4pm
summary: A cafe and micro roastery that roasts its coffee on site, with brunch and lunch from the menu and cabinet, and gluten-free options. A few minutes from Te Pae.

name: Rook
access_notes: Mon-Fri 7am-2pm, closed weekends
summary: A sleek, modern cafe on the ground floor of Malvern House on Hereford Street. Weekdays only, from early morning to early afternoon.

name: Grizzly Baked Goods
access_notes: Mon-Fri 7:30am-2:30pm, closed weekends
summary: Bagels and baked goods from a crew that started with a Christchurch Farmers Market stall in 2013. Handy for the Canterbury Earthquake National Memorial, a short walk away.

name: The Church Pub
access_notes: Daily from 11am, until 11pm Sun-Wed and 1am Thu-Sat
summary: A brew bar inside Benjamin Mountfort's former Trinity Congregational Church (about 1875), his first church in stone. Badly damaged in February 2011 and since restored, it is a heritage stop in its own right.
story:
Trinity Congregational Church was built around 1873-1875 to a design by Benjamin Mountfort, the architect of the Provincial Council Buildings and Canterbury Museum. It was his first church in stone and is a Category 1 heritage building. Its octagonal central space sits under a timber-panelled double-barrel vault that has been called one of Mountfort's most impressive and original inventions.

The church was seriously damaged in the 22 February 2011 earthquake and sat cordoned off for years before being restored. It now houses The Church Pub, a brew bar, on the corner of Worcester and Manchester Streets, so you can see the restored interior over a drink.

name: OGB
access_notes: Mon-Thu 3pm-1am, Fri-Sun 12pm-1am
summary: A bar in the early-1900s Old Government Building on Cathedral Square, with staff in period dress, tables out by the tram line, and anything from snacks to bistro plates.

name: The Last Word
access_notes: Mon-Wed 4pm-11pm, Thu-Fri 4pm-late, Sat 4pm-2am, Sun hours vary
summary: A whisky and cocktail bar on New Regent Street, the 1930s Spanish Mission street that was restored after the earthquakes. A good place to finish a walk.

name: Imōto Lounge Bar
access_notes: Tue-Sat 2pm-11pm, closed Sun-Mon
summary: The 'little sister' to Bar Yoku at The Welder: a low-lit lounge with bold cocktails and small plates that mix Kiwi classics with Japanese izakaya dishes.
